items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-08-06
items.q: I consider Freddie one of the finest drummers that I've ever had the opportunity of working with.

ctx.x: Well, I'm trying to notice everything, you know. Well, that's great. You're inquisitive. You told me about how nothing was rehearsed yesterday. That amazed me because the band, you know, everything was so pretty. All the hominis seemed right to me, you know.

Right. Well, we rehearsed but not at the place. We rehearsed over the telephone. Oh. How did I do that? Yeah. Okay. I discussed it with Freddie Coleman. I told him, I said, you know what I want you to do, don't you? What? I said, well, I want you to do the same thing that you did last year. Bring that tambourine and watch my tempos. Well, I tell you to cut him and cut out and just listen to me. And he laughed. He says, okay. So, I did the same thing with Walter Lewis, but Walter had just recently played a concert…
So, you had no problem. It's just the guys worked together. Right. And they knew that I could play three-part harmony if you wanted them.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-12-30
items.q: I had a number of drummers... Freddie Coleman doesn't increase. He doesn't drop back. Freddie plays identical drums to Fats Martin... But sometimes a drummer that's, what we call a show drummer... He has a tendency of increasing or decreasing.

ctx.x: And of course that's, we just scratching the surface when we start talking about the foys of your band and everything. How many drummers have you known that didn't increase? How many of them?

I had a number of drummers. A lot of drummers don't increase. Freddie Coleman doesn't increase. He doesn't drop back. Freddie plays identical drums to Fats Martin, which the only difference of his tempo is more sustainable. But sometimes a drummer that's, what we call a show drummer, that's showing out in other words. He has a tendency of increasing or decreasing. Because he's too wrapped up in what he wants to do and then he gets away from the basic part. Well, what you have was, well Joe Jones. Joe Jones never…
Well, to me, most drummers now, it seems, increase. And, for example, that they don't make drummers like they do.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: if you close the curtain in front of Freddie Coleman, and close your eyes, you'd hear Fats Martin.

ctx.x: You had to change the style of the band, yeah. Yeah.

But there was always that, they said, there's something about this band that makes you want to dance. Well, I've got to give credit to Fats Martin. Now, if you close the curtain in front of Freddie Coleman, and close your eyes, you'd hear Fats Martin. It's almost identical. Fats Martin was the greatest drumming that I've ever heard. And he set the tempos. And it was something, now and then a fast number, which people would try to dance on, but they couldn't. It was mostly a feature number that featured musicians.

What about, I can't remember if I've answered this before. People in New Orleans have another language, I mean, not just the Creoles, but the whole, they picked up a lot of French and Spanish things here. What about in Texas? Do they say any of the same words over there? What do they say?
